sentences.text: This pterosaur possessed an estimated wingspan of 2.4 meters, a large size for a basal pterodactyloid.
Its skull measured between 390 and 400 millimeters in length, appearing extremely elongated with a slightly concave top.
The jaws held seventy-six long, curved, needle-like teeth restricted to the front third of the mouth.
In one specimen, the neck vertebrae were very elongated, measuring five times longer than they were wide.
The genus was named and described in 2005 by Wang Xiaolin, Alexander Kellner, Zhou Zhonghe, and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.
The specific name youngi honors the Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian.
The type specimen is holotype IVPP V-12539, a crushed skull and articulated mandible of a subadult individual.
A second specimen, DNMHM D3068, found at Gonggao in 2014, was referred to Feilongus.
Ctenochasmatoids like Feilongus are hypothesized to have used their numerous small, thin teeth to strain food from water, similar to flamingos.
If Feilongus is classified within the Ornithocheiroidea sensu Unwin, its members are typically adapted for soaring and a fish-eating diet.
A 2018 phylogenetic analysis places Feilongus as a ctenochasmatid in the subfamily Moganopterinae with its sister taxon Moganopterus.
Feilongus lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous in the Yixian Formation of Beipiao, Liaoning, China.
Feilongus lived between 125.77 and 113.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether Feilongus is an archaeopterodactyloid or a member of the Ornithocheiroidea closer to the Anhangueridae, based on a 2006 analysis by Lü Junchang.
Some researchers have proposed placing Feilongus and Boreopterus in a new family called Boreopteridae.
